process: D20: two blind graders (D7), adjudicator on disagreements, agent audit of agreed verdicts (D11)

verdicts.reason: Wikipedia (citing PwC/Strategy&) confirms 21% of large public companies had a CDO by 2020, but that measures CDO presence, not CIOs supplanted by a CDO for digital product delivery; no survey of the same population and behaviour exists for 2019-2020 (session rule, D22/D23 same-quantity), so the bound argument does not support a published verdict.

Looked for a public 2016-2017 value of 3rd Platform share of IT spending. IDC's public Black Book releases opened now (CEMA release 2017-04-28 via Wayback; Business Wire release 2017-10-18 via Wayback; Black Book 3rd Platform Highlights PDF, 2018-03) give only forecasts (3rd Platform 75% of ICT spending by 2021), total ICT ($4.3T in 2016) and 'the 2nd Platform still represents more than $1 trillion in annual ICT spending today'. That last figure is a lower bound for 2017 ICT (incl. telecom services and consumer spend), not organizations' IT spending, and gives no 3rd Platform share; deriving a share from it would be a proxy of another scope (D23). The only public measured share found by grader B is ~29% for 2014. No public measure at the target year: ungradable.

The earlier block (Okta Secure Sign-in Trends pages returned 404) is now cleared: the 2023 report's executive summary PDF opened. It reports MFA adoption as a share of Okta Workforce Identity users (about 65% by end of 2022 per the report; by country 25-79%; 54% at 20,000+ employee firms). That is a share of workforce users at Okta customers, not a share of CIOs or organizations, and covers workforce sign-in, not ecosystem-wide (partner and customer) MFA. Using it would grade a different population and quantity (D23 proxy). No public 2021-2022 survey of the share of organizations requiring MFA across their ecosystem was found: ungradable.

Still ungradable (D23 conditional claim). Condition first: public cloud (the core of 'as a service') is about $723B of roughly $5.6T IT spending in 2025, about 13% (Gartner). Whether the condition held depends on whether managed and outsourced services count as 'as a service'; no public series measures IDC's aaS share, so the condition is not shown to hold. The consequent (size of lasting opex resets) has no public measure either. Note: the earlier graders cite US49563122, the IT Industry 2023 edition; the claim is from the CIO Agenda 2023 FutureScape.

Still ungradable (D23). No public series gives AI as a share of core IT spend for the G2000. ISG's survey of 300 G2000 executives (Oct-Nov 2024) reports only that AI is 30% of the 2025 budget increase and AI spend grows 5.7% vs 1.8% for IT, not the level share. Related estimates disagree by far more than a factor of 2: Oxford Economics puts AI under 4% of enterprise tech spend in 2025 (all enterprises, model-based); BCG AI Radar has large firms planning AI spend of about 5% of revenue, which would be comparable to or above typical IT budgets. Under D23 (scope not matched; estimates span >2x) this stays ungradable, though every estimate found sits well below 40%.

Opened the pages the earlier pass could not: Gartner's 2023 CIO survey (n=2,457) reports 70% call GenAI game-changing, 9% deployed, 55% plan to within 24 months: attitude and plans, not pressure. Salesforce/Vanson Bourne (600 IT professionals, Dec 2023-Jan 2024) says GenAI is the #1 technology IT feels pressure to onboard quickly and 88% cannot keep up with AI requests, but gives no share of CIOs feeling pressure. RWS reports 87% of C-suite executives feel pressure, a different population. EY 2024 US CIO sentiment survey has no pressure share. No measure of this population and behaviour.

Session rule: a share of CIOs is gradable against a survey of the same population and behaviour at the target year or the year before. The 2025 Gartner CIO and Technology Executive Survey (3,186 CIOs and technology executives, 88 countries, fielded 2024, published October 2024) reports 37% of organizations had already deployed GenAI. Error |35-37|/37 = 5.4%: hit under D16 numeric. Grader A's factor-of-2 range mixes populations and years: the Gartner Q4 2023 survey (29%) and McKinsey State of AI (about 65%) are not CIO surveys, and the 2024 CIO survey (9% deployed) was fielded in 2023 and is superseded by the target-year survey of the same population. With same-population data only, D23's range test does not trigger. Uncertainty: the 37% figure was confirmed via search results only (Gartner pages return 403 to fetch); a broader reading of 'embrace' (deployed or piloting) is not measured by any CIO survey and would not lower the verdict below partial.

Still ungradable (D22/D23). No public 2024-2025 CIO survey gives a share motivated or planning to automate compliance and ESG reporting. Looked for: Gartner, Foundry, IDC CIO surveys on compliance/ESG automation.

Still ungradable (D22/D23). No public survey of the G1000 (or the largest firms) measures difficulty with divergent regulation in 2025. Looked for: IDC, Gartner, KPMG/EY large-enterprise regulatory surveys giving this share. Note: earlier graders cite US51736824, the IT Industry 2025 edition; the claim is from the CIO Agenda 2025 FutureScape.

Surveys of organizations measuring this behaviour exist for 2024 and 2025, so grader A's 'no such survey found' is a search gap. Estimates on the dominant reading (in place or in progress): IAPP, spring 2024, 77% working on AI governance; Pacific AI, Feb-May 2025, 75% have AI usage policies; PEX Report 2025/26, 43% have an AI governance policy plus 25% implementing one = 68%. Range 68-77%, within a factor of 2 (D23). Median 75%; |85-75|/75 = 13.3%: partial. Grader B's median of two (76%, 11.8%) gives the same verdict. Narrower readings (formal governance framework 36%, dedicated role 59%, risk-evaluation process 45%) would be a miss, but 'be formalizing' is progressive and names policies first, so the broad reading dominates. Sample caveat: all three are self-selected professional surveys, not representative panels.

Still ungradable (D23). Found IDC's 2023/2024 CIO Sentiment Survey via CIO.com: nearly 4 in 10 CIOs expected to overspend on digital infrastructure and 47% of those blamed tech debt; CIOs ranked tech debt elimination well below AI and security. Neither is the share of CIOs driving enterprise remediation initiatives, and it predates the target year. Gartner's '<20% of software leaders are very effective at managing tech debt' is another construct. No measure of the claim's quantity. Note: earlier graders cite US51736824, the IT Industry 2025 edition; the claim is from the CIO Agenda 2025 FutureScape.
